## Results

### Whole-spectrum clustering and the no-peak reference

#### K-means clusterisation {#result-clusterisation}

In the iEEG atlas the clustering resolved distinct, band-specific peak groups. With the 0.5–80 Hz bandpass of @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial applied, it reproduced their eight-group solution: a no-peak group and seven peak groups spanning low delta, high delta, theta, alpha, low beta, high beta, and gamma. Removing the bandpass reduced this to seven groups — a no-peak group and six peak clusters (two delta, one theta, two alpha, one beta) — with no gamma group and no low/high-beta split (@fig-clusters B). We decided to use option withous bandpass filtering,  as  discussed in @sec-clustering..

Source-reconstructed HD-EEG produced a markedly different structure of eleven groups. Seven carried a peak in the alpha range (8–12 Hz) and differed only in amplitude, so the procedure over-segmented a single alpha-dominated continuum rather than resolving separate bands (@fig-clusters C); no distinct theta or beta cluster emerged, and the no-peak cluster was flatter than its iEEG counterpart.

We labelled each cluster by the frequency of its maximum deviation from the no-peak baseline (interpretable only where a genuine peak is present),  only the δ and α HD-EEG clusters showed a clear bump above the aperiodic background. The remaining high-frequency clusters were separated by a shallower aperiodic slope and an elevated broadband tail, not by an oscillation. Where the iEEG atlas resolved oscillatory clusters from δ to γ, the HD-EEG structure reduced to alpha power and aperiodic slope (@fig-clusters).

![We show spectral clustering in iEEG and source-reconstructed HD-EEG. Panel A is the average raw (non-normalised) PSD for each modality. Panels B and C show the cluster solutions on normalised spectra: the seven iEEG clusters (B) and the eleven HD-EEG clusters (C), each including one no-peak cluster. A knee is visible in the iEEG clusters, whereas the reconstructed sources are closer to 1/f.](figures/chapter2/clusters/rawpower_and_clusters.pdf){#fig-clusters width="100%" column="page"}

Testing each region against the no-peak set across the 22 frequency intervals reproduced this contrast at regional resolution (@fig-stat-reg_dfiff). In the iEEG atlas, regions deviated from the no-peak distribution across the whole spectrum and in a regionally specific way: the alpha interval was strongest in occipital cortex — up to all channels in the cuneus and ~0.86 in superior and middle occipital gyri — parietal regions extended the deviation into beta (postcentral gyrus ~0.73), precentral and frontal regions carried beta and low-gamma peaks (precentral up to ~0.5 at 15-30 Hz), and the hippocampus deviated specifically in the delta range (~0.44-0.69 at 1-3 Hz). In source-reconstructed HD-EEG the significant channels collapsed onto a single alpha column (~8-13 Hz), shared across almost all regions at comparable fractions (~0.5-0.79); the delta, theta and beta intervals were essentially empty, and the only further deviation was an isolated high-frequency column (31.75-80 Hz, with some 20-31 Hz) at moderate fractions (~0.4-0.53) that tracks the elevated broadband tail rather than a rhythm.

![Regional differences from the no-peak set across frequency intervals, for iEEG (A) and source-reconstructed HD-EEG (B). Cell coloring is the fraction of a region's channels whose relative power exceeded the no-peak distribution.](figures/chapter2/clusters/combined_regional_differences_faceted.pdf){#fig-stat-reg_dfiff width="100%" column="page"}

The same divergence appears in the lobar mean spectra overlaid on the no-peak reference (@fig-lobar-reg_dfiff). In iEEG every lobe rose above the reference with a clear alpha peak — tallest and broadest in occipital cortex — alongside additional theta and beta structure in the frontal and temporal lobes, a multimodal departure from the background. In HD-EEG each lobe instead reduced to a single sharp alpha peak, strongest in occipital and parietal lobes, with the significantly deviating frequencies confined to the alpha band and no separate theta or beta elevation.

![Lobar differences relative to the no-peak set, for iEEG (top) and source-reconstructed HD-EEG (bottom). We overlay each lobe's mean normalised spectrum on the no-peak reference; n per lobe is annotated.](figures/chapter2/clusters/combined_lobar_differences_faceted.pdf){#fig-lobar-reg_dfiff width="100%" column="page"}

#### Clustering stability and data driven intervals 

We next evaluated the stability of the clustering solution, the no-peak reference set, and the data-driven frequency intervals used for regional peak detection. These components were sensitive to preprocessing choices and to the fitted frequency range: small changes in the lower or upper bound altered the number of clusters and the membership and shape of the no-peak reference set. This was worst in the source-reconstructed HD-EEG data, where some configurations failed to produce a no-peak set at all.

The data-driven intervals also failed to transfer. @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial defined 22 intervals so that each held at least 4% of the total mean power in iEEG; applied to the HD-EEG spectra, the same rule yielded 21 intervals and split the range above 31.75 Hz into five separate intervals, where the atlas defined a single 31.75-80 Hz band. We attributed this gamma over-segmentation to the unit-power normalisation (see Discussion). Because the rule did not transfer, we retained the fixed 22 intervals of @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial for both modalities to keep them comparable.

For this reason the 4% condition does not transfer to source-reconstructed data, and data-driven HD-EEG intervals are not directly comparable with the iEEG atlas. To preserve cross-modal comparability, the fixed 22 intervals of @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial were retained for both modalities in all regional peak-detection tests (@fig-stat-reg_dfiff ).

The clustering, the no-peak reference, and the power-based interval definition were therefore potentially unstable across reasonable preprocessing choices. We did not apply this k-means descriptor to the aperiodic-corrected (`specparam`) spectra. In the subsequent analyses we instead characterised oscillatory content with the per-band parametrised-peak descriptor, which needs neither a clustering step nor a no-peak reference and was therefore less dependent on these preprocessing choices.

###  Normalised relative-power maps before and after broadband correction

We present regional relative band power, compared across modalities, with the band- and interval-overlap metric. We read it in two states — on the uncorrected spectra in @sec-normarive-uncorrected and after removing the specparam aperiodic component (@sec-normarive-corrected).

#### Band-power map on uncorrected spectra  {#sec-normarive-uncorrected}

We mapped each region's relative band power on the uncorrected unit-power spectra, as a fraction of total power within each canonical band and each Frauscher interval; per region we summarise across its channels — the group mean on the surface maps, the median in the heatmaps. We show it in two views: the band-wise spatial distribution projected onto the cortical surface (@fig-relpower-maps-uncorrected), and the full region × band matrix as heatmaps, for both band schemes and both modalities (@fig-relpower-heatmaps). The wide canonical bands carry a much larger fraction of total power than the narrow Frauscher intervals, so each heatmap panel is scaled to its own maximum and colour is not comparable across panels. In both modalities the delta band carries the largest fraction of total power — the steep 1/f tail, not a rhythm. The clearest band-limited elevation is a posterior alpha focus, sharper in HD-EEG, and the HD-EEG heatmap additionally shows elevated power in the highest Frauscher interval (31.75-80 Hz) that the iEEG atlas lacks. Relative band powers are compositional: the bands within a channel sum to a fixed total.

![Group-average relative PSD per ROI, faceted by canonical band (columns) and modality (rows: iEEG top, HD-EEG source bottom). Colour is the within-band relative power (fraction of total power) on a single shared scale across all panels, so magnitude is comparable across bands and modalities — delta highest, gamma lowest. Hippocampus and amygdala have no cortical-surface geometry in the Frauscher ggsegpy atlas and are not shown.](figures/chapter2/relative_power/relpower_maps_uncorrected.pdf){#fig-relpower-maps-uncorrected}



![Median relative band power per bilateral region, before aperiodic correction, as region × band heatmaps. Modalities are stacked — iEEG (top, A-B) over HD-EEG (bottom, C-D) — with the five canonical bands (left) and the 22 Frauscher intervals (right, @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial) across the columns, so each band scheme aligns vertically between modalities. The value in each cell is the median across the region's channels of the within-band relative power (band power as a fraction of total power, so in [0, 1]); each panel has its own colorbar, auto-scaled to its maximum, because the wide canonical bands carry a much larger fraction of total power than the narrow Frauscher bins. Rows are bilateral MICCAI regions grouped by lobe, with lobe-coloured labels.](figures/chapter2/relative_power/relpower_heatmaps_uncorrected.pdf){#fig-relpower-heatmaps}

#### Crossmodal correlation and and cross-modal overlap comparison on uncorrected spectra

Regional relative-power maps agreed across modalities most strongly in the alpha band (r = 0.60) and, more weakly, in the delta band (r = 0.42). Theta showed essentially no cross-modal correspondence (r = 0.13), beta only weak agreement (r = 0.30), and gamma was anti-correlated (r = −0.29). The spatial organisation of relative power is therefore only partially preserved between the iEEG atlas and source-reconstructed HD-EEG, and the preservation is band-dependent: it is confined largely to the alpha and low-frequency ranges that carry the clearest oscillatory structure, and breaks down at high frequencies.

Points are coloured by lobe, the solid line is the per-band OLS fit, and the dashed line marks identity (y = x). Strip labels give the per-band Pearson correlation.](figures/chapter2/relative_power/relpower_scatter_uncorrected.pdf){#fig-relpower-scatter-uncorrected}

These per-band correlations are descriptive rather than inferential: the regions are not independent and the relative powers are compositional (Methods), so we base formal cross-modal inference on the bootstrap overlap below and on the peak descriptors.

To compare directly with the clustering analysis, we recomputed the overlap in the same heatmap display (@fig-overlap-pair-uncorrected). The overlap is strongest in the delta and alpha bands, with beta present in some regions. Cells are masked where the bootstrap 95% CI of the overlap includes zero, and a contrast dot marks cells where a reliable overlap sits on a flat residual — a reliable agreement with no significant rhythm in either modality, which matters for the presence-conditioned analysis below.

Each bilateral MICCAI region is coloured by its band-averaged Afnan overlap on a fixed 0-1 scale — the metric is already bounded, so colour is comparable across bands and across regions; the strip reports the per-band mean overlap across regions. Hippocampus and amygdala have no cortical-surface geometry in the Frauscher ggsegpy atlas and are not shown.](figures/chapter2/relative_power/overlap_maps_uncorrected.pdf){#fig-overlap-maps-uncorrected}

Both panels are masked (grey) where the bootstrap 95% CI of the overlap includes 0 and carry a contrast dot where a reliable overlap sits on a flat residual (no significant rhythm in either modality — spurious agreement).](figures/chapter2/relative_power/overlap_pair_uncorrected.pdf){#fig-overlap-pair-uncorrected}



#### Aperiodic-removed band power {#sec-normarive-corrected}

We now repeat the same three views on the periodic part of the spectrum. Each channel is fit with specparam in its BIC-selected aperiodic mode (knee for iEEG, fixed for HD-EEG), and the fitted aperiodic component is subtracted from the normalised spectrum, so the per-band value is the channel's oscillatory power in that band as a fraction of total power, on the same footing as the uncorrected relative band power above

The specparam model captured the aperiodic background well in the iEEG atlas: across the 1772 channels the knee model reached a mean R² of 0.98 (± 0.01; median 0.985, only 4 channels below 0.90), with a mean offset of 5.10 ± 1.57 and an exponent of 3.39 ± 0.88, and a median knee frequency of 11.2 Hz (IQR 7.8-15.9). The fixed model on the 1444 source-reconstructed HD-EEG channels fit less well and far more variably (mean R² 0.91 ± 0.11, median 0.94; 376/1444 channels, 26%, fell below 0.90), with a much lower offset (−2.79 ± 0.58) and a shallower exponent (0.94 ± 0.33). Mean absolute error was comparable across modalities (0.087 vs 0.073 in log₁₀ power). The substantially poorer and more dispersed HD-EEG fits, together with the shallow exponent, indicate that the HD-EEG aperiodic estimate — and hence its oscillatory residual — is less reliable than the iEEG one.

<!-- We now repeat the same three views on the periodic part of the spectrum. Each channel is fit with specparam in its BIC-selected aperiodic mode (knee for iEEG, fixed for HD-EEG), and the fitted aperiodic component is subtracted from the normalised spectrum, so the per-band value is the channel's oscillatory power in that band as a fraction of total power — directly comparable to the uncorrected relative band power above. -->

Removing the aperiodic background isolates the rhythmic peaks from the $1/f$ tail, so the correspondence is no longer inflated (or, in gamma, depressed) by the steepness of the background. The closure constraint still applies — the linear residual is normalised to total power — so these per-band correlations remain descriptive.

The fitted aperiodic parameters summarise each modality's $1/f$ background — iEEG fit with a knee, HD-EEG with the fixed (knee-free) model. Offset and exponent are mean ± sd across channels; the knee is reported as the knee *frequency* ($\text{knee}^{1/\chi}$, in Hz) as median [IQR], since the raw knee parameter is heavy-tailed (a few channels push the knee out of band).

| modality | n channels | offset | exponent | knee freq (Hz) | R² (mean) |

| iEEG (knee) | 1772 | 5.096 ± 1.570 | 3.392 ± 0.884 | 11.23 [7.76, 15.92] | 0.982 |
| HD-EEG (fixed) | 1444 | -2.787 ± 0.577 | 0.944 ± 0.325 | — | 0.908 |

#### Crossmodal correlation and and cross-modal overlap comparison on corrected spectra

Across the 38 bilateral regions the oscillatory-residual maps corresponded most strongly in the alpha band (r = 0.65), with weaker positive correspondence in delta (r = 0.35), theta (r = 0.24) and beta (r = 0.26), and a negative correlation in gamma (r = −0.26; @fig-relpower-scatter-corrected). In alpha the occipital and parietal regions carry the largest residual in both modalities, but the per-band fit sits below the identity line — for a given region the HD-EEG residual exceeds the atlas, i.e. source HD-EEG carries proportionally more alpha.

Under the confidence-interval masking, reliable overlap of the aperiodic-removed spectra concentrated in delta and alpha across most regions, with beta in a subset; on the 22 Frauscher intervals most higher-frequency cells were masked (@fig-overlap-pair-corrected). Conditioning instead on rhythm presence, the cells where both modalities carried a genuine rhythm were concentrated in alpha — high overlap in posterior regions — with some delta, whereas many beta and gamma cells were marked where the iEEG atlas carried a rhythm that source HD-EEG did not recover, most often in frontal and temporal regions (@fig-overlap-corr-presence-gated-pair).

Each panel is one canonical band; each point is one bilateral MICCAI region, source HD-EEG oscillatory residual on x and the iEEG atlas on y. Points are coloured by lobe, the solid line is the per-band OLS fit, and the dashed line marks identity (y = x). The residual is the specparam linear oscillatory power (band fraction of total) with the BIC-selected aperiodic component removed.](figures/chapter2/relative_power/relpower_scatter_corrected.pdf){#fig-relpower-scatter-corrected}



In the residual spectra the band-overlap was strongest in delta and alpha across most regions, present in beta in a subset, and weakest in gamma (@fig-overlap-pair-corrected, A); on the 22 Frauscher intervals the reliable cells concentrated in the low-frequency and alpha intervals, with much of the higher-frequency range masked where the bootstrap interval included zero (B).
![Aperiodic-removed cross-modal overlap. A) five canonical EEG bands B) the 22 intervals defined in @frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial. Both panels are masked (grey) where the bootstrap 95% CI of the overlap includes 0 and carry a contrast dot where a reliable overlap sits on a flat residual (no significant rhythm in either modality — spurious agreement).](figures/chapter2/relative_power/overlap_pair_corrected.pdf){#fig-overlap-pair-corrected}

#### Presence-conditioned overlap (peaks-presence bootstrap)

As an alternative to conditioning on the overlap's own confidence interval, we condition on whether a rhythm is actually present. This uses the same subject-clustered bootstrap of the oscillatory-residual band power (95% CI > 0), referenced to the iEEG atlas, to drive the canonical-band overlap shown in @fig-overlap-corr-presence-gated-pair.

Conditioning on rhythm presence restricts the comparison to cells where both modalities carry a genuine rhythm (@fig-overlap-corr-presence-gated-pair). These concentrate in the alpha band — high overlap in posterior regions — together with some delta, whereas many beta and gamma cells are marked where the iEEG atlas carries a rhythm that HD-EEG did not recover, most often in frontal and temporal regions.



![Presence-conditioned cross-modal overlap of the aperiodic-removed residual, the two band schemes side by side: five canonical EEG bands (left) and the 22 Frauscher intervals (right), at their natural asymmetric width. In both panels the Afnan overlap is coloured only where a subject-clustered bootstrap (whole subjects resampled — iEEG patients, HD datasets; 95% CI of the mean residual band power excludes 0) finds a rhythm in **both** modalities; cells are masked where no rhythm is present in both and marked × where the iEEG atlas carries a rhythm that HD-EEG did not recover. Same renderer as the confidence-interval pair (@fig-overlap-pair-corrected); only the masking rule differs (presence rather than the overlap's confidence interval), and the band scheme differs between panels.](figures/chapter2/relative_power/overlap_pair_corrected_presencegated.pdf){#fig-overlap-corr-presence-gated-pair}

#### Cross-modal overlap before and after aperiodic correction

Removing the aperiodic component changes the cross-modal picture, and the change depends on how the oscillatory residual is defined. We computed the per-lobe oscillatory spectrum in 2 Hz bins under four extractors — the detrended residual and the modelled (specparam-peak) power, each in a log and a linear form — and compared modalities with a subject-clustered bootstrap (per-lobe mean ± 95% CI, @fig-residual-state) and a frequency cluster-permutation test (Maris-Oostenveld, resampling whole subjects) that controls the family-wise error across frequency (@fig-residual-diff).

The **modelled** rhythmic power — the measure that does not depend on the accuracy of the aperiodic fit — shows iEEG and HD-EEG differing in a contiguous beta/low-gamma cluster (~25-48 Hz, iEEG higher) across most lobes, and a parietal alpha cluster (~10-12 Hz) where HD-EEG is higher; occipital high-gamma is again higher in iEEG. The **detrended residual** reproduces the beta excess but adds a broad high-frequency cluster (~55-80 Hz) in which HD-EEG appears systematically higher than iEEG across every lobe. This high-frequency block is present in the residual but absent from the modelled measure, identifying it as aperiodic-tail/noise leakage rather than a rhythm — exactly the conflation that @castanheira2026AnalyticalChoicesImpact predict for detrended spectra.
<!-- REVIEW: "exactly the conflation that ... predict" overstates the match. "the kind of conflation ... describe" is safer. -->
 The log and linear residuals agree on the sign and location of the clusters but differ in magnitude, as expected from their different units.

We therefore read the modelled-peak comparison as the substantive cross-modal result: the rhythms that survive aperiodic separation correspond across modalities chiefly in the alpha band, with a beta/low-gamma offset, whereas the apparent high-frequency cross-modal difference in the subtraction residual is an artefact of the aperiodic background rather than a difference in oscillatory activity.

![Per-lobe oscillatory power in 2 Hz bins (subject-clustered bootstrap mean ± 95% CI), for the four extractors (rows: detrended residual / modelled, in log and linear form) and the two modalities (columns). Lines coloured by lobe.](figures/chapter2/peaks/lobe_oscillatory_state_bootstrap.pdf){#fig-residual-state width="100%" column="page"}

![Cross-modal difference (iEEG − HD-EEG) per extractor: Welch $t$ over lobe × 2 Hz bin; black dots mark frequency clusters significant under subject-level permutation ($p<0.05$, family-wise controlled). The high-frequency HD-higher cluster appears only in the residual, not the modelled, rows.](figures/chapter2/peaks/lobe_oscillatory_diff_bootstrap.pdf){#fig-residual-diff width="80%" column="page"}

### Directly modelled specparam peaks

#### Description of distribution of peaks

**Centre frequency and dominant rhythm.** Because canonical-band assignment is sensitive to peaks near a band edge, we also examined the fitted centre frequencies directly. The HD-EEG centre-frequency distribution is a sharp alpha mode at ~10 Hz, sitting squarely against the 8 and 13 Hz band edges, whereas iEEG peaks are broadly distributed with an additional high-gamma cluster near 70 Hz (@fig-centre-freq). The per-region dominant peak frequency — the centre frequency of the single highest-amplitude peak — is alpha-locked across almost all regions in HD-EEG but scatters into beta and gamma for several frontal and temporal regions in iEEG (@fig-dominant-dumbbell). The full per-region distribution of peak frequencies confirms a narrow posterior alpha ridge in HD against broader, multimodal iEEG ridges (@fig-region-ridges).

![Distribution of fitted peak centre frequencies per modality, against the canonical band edges (dashed). HD-EEG shows a single sharp ~10 Hz alpha mode; iEEG is broad with a high-gamma cluster.](figures/chapter2/peaks/peak_centre_frequency_distribution.pdf){#fig-centre-freq width="80%"}

![Dominant peak frequency per region: the centre frequency of the highest-amplitude peak, connecting iEEG (blue) and source HD-EEG (red) for each region. Regions follow the lobe order and colouring of the heatmaps.](figures/chapter2/peaks/dominant_frequency_dumbbell.pdf){#fig-dominant-dumbbell width="70%"}

![Per-region distribution of peak centre frequencies (histogram ridgeline, normalised per region), filled by lobe. HD-EEG (right) is a narrow posterior alpha ridge; iEEG (left) is broader and multimodal.](figures/chapter2/peaks/region_frequency_ridges.pdf){#fig-region-ridges width="100%" column="page"}

Pooling all regions, <!-- REVIEW: "makes the contrast immediate" — LLM flourish. Cut or replace with neutral "shows". -->
the joint distribution of peak amplitude and centre frequency (@fig-size-freq) makes the contrast immediate: HD-EEG peaks form one dense high-amplitude alpha mode at ~10 Hz with a sparse low-amplitude tail above it, whereas iEEG peaks spread along the frequency axis at moderate amplitude, with a distinct beta/low-gamma body and a high-gamma cluster near 70 Hz.

![Peak size (amplitude) vs centre frequency, binned density per modality (all regions pooled). HD-EEG is a single high-amplitude alpha mode; iEEG is spread across frequency with a high-gamma cluster.](figures/chapter2/peaks/peak_size_vs_frequency.pdf){#fig-size-freq width="100%" column="page"}

Jointly resolving peak amplitude and centre frequency per lobe (@fig-size-freq-lobe) confirms that the two descriptors are not redundant. In HD-EEG the per-channel peak density concentrates into a single tall alpha column in occipital and parietal lobes — high amplitude at ~10 Hz — and thins sharply elsewhere. In iEEG the density is spread along the frequency axis at moderate amplitude, with frontal and temporal lobes carrying beta and low-gamma peaks that have no HD-EEG counterpart. Normalising to peaks per channel makes the lobes comparable despite their different channel counts, and shows the cross-modal divergence is one of *where in the spectrum* rhythms occur, not merely how strong they are.

![Peak size (amplitude) vs centre frequency, binned density per lobe (rows) and modality (columns), normalised to peaks per channel so lobes of different size are comparable. HD-EEG concentrates in a posterior alpha column; iEEG spreads across frequency, with frontal/temporal beta-gamma.](figures/chapter2/peaks/peak_size_vs_frequency_by_lobe.pdf){#fig-size-freq-lobe width="100%" column="page"}

#### Peaks prevalence

Once oscillations are modelled explicitly, peak prevalence — the fraction of a region's channels carrying at least one fitted peak in a band — diverges sharply between modalities (@fig-peak-prevalence). Source HD-EEG is dominated by alpha: mean prevalence across regions is 0.63 in alpha but only 0.11 in theta, 0.05 in gamma and 0.01 in delta. The iEEG atlas is broader, with substantial beta (0.40), gamma (0.26) and alpha (0.24) prevalence. The difference map (HD − iEEG) is strongly positive in alpha — HD detects alpha peaks far more often, especially in posterior regions — and negative across beta and gamma, where iEEG detects high-frequency peaks that the source fit does not recover.

Cross-modal agreement of the regional prevalence *pattern* (Spearman across the 38 bilateral regions) is confined to the low and mid bands: alpha $\rho = 0.60$ and beta $\rho = 0.47$, against delta $\rho = 0.04$, theta $\rho = -0.07$ and gamma $\rho = -0.25$ (@fig-prevalence-scatter). In alpha the points sit above the identity line — HD detects alpha in more regions than iEEG — yet the two modalities still rank regions consistently. This mirrors the uncorrected relative-band-power result (alpha strongest, gamma anti-correlated), now with the aperiodic background modelled out rather than carried in the power.

Because modelled power exists only where a peak is fitted, prevalence is also the peak-detection rate and must be read alongside the amplitude and centre-frequency descriptors. Mean peaks per channel were similar across modalities (iEEG 1.45, HD 1.37 under the main settings), but 99.7% of iEEG channels passed the $R^2 > 0.9$ screen against only 74.0% of HD channels, with the missing HD peaks concentrated in the high-frequency bands where the source spectrum is flattest.

Each point is a bilateral region; dashed line is identity; strip labels give the per-band Spearman $\rho$ across regions.](figures/chapter2/peaks/peak_prevalence_agreement_scatter.pdf){#fig-prevalence-scatter width="100%" column="page"}

**Modelled power.** <!-- REVIEW: "tells the same story in amplitude that prevalence tells in detection" — LLM-style parallelism/cliché. State the finding directly. -->
The amplitude of the highest peak per band (median across the channels that carry a peak) tells the same story in amplitude that prevalence tells in detection: posterior alpha carries the largest modelled power in HD-EEG, while in iEEG the amplitude is spread across beta in frontal and central regions (@fig-modelled-power).

![Modelled band power by region and modality: median amplitude (log-power height above the aperiodic component) of the highest peak in each band, over channels with a detected peak.](figures/chapter2/peaks/modelled_power_heatmap.pdf){#fig-modelled-power width="100%" column="page"}
